title: Absence of Route-Level Throttle Middleware on Auth and Public API Endpoints
description: Key authentication actions (login, register, forgot-password) and the public tracking API route lack route-level rate limiting middleware (throttle), permitting high-velocity automated enumeration and request flooding.
root_cause: In routes/web.php and routes/api.php, routes for POST /login, POST /register, POST /forgot-password, and GET /api/v1/track/{transaction_code} are not assigned the 'throttle' middleware or named rate limiters.
intended_behavior: Public unauthenticated endpoints and sensitive authentication handlers should be guarded by rate limiters (e.g., throttle:5,1 for login, throttle:60,1 for public tracking API).

trace.description: POST /login route definition without throttle middleware.
GET /api/v1/track/{transaction_code} route definition without route throttle.
Public endpoint executes database lookup on every unthrottled incoming request.

conditions.description: Attacker can send high volumes of HTTP requests directly to the web or API endpoints.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unauthenticated remote attacker performs automated brute-force attacks or enumerates existing transaction codes.
payloads: for i in {1..100}; do curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/login -d 'email=test@example.com&password=wrong'; done
instructions: Send 20 consecutive POST requests to /login within 5 seconds with invalid credentials.
Observe whether HTTP 429 Too Many Requests is returned by route middleware or if full execution occurs.
execution.observed_result: Requests bypass route-level rate limiting, executing full request pipeline.

remediation.strategy: Attach named or inline throttle middleware (throttle:5,1 for login, throttle:60,1 for API) to protect authentication and tracking routes.

likelihood.reason: Public endpoints are accessible to anyone on the internet without credentials.

impact.reason: Resource consumption and password guessing attempts; mitigated internally by LoginRequest attempt checks.

confidence.reason: Confirmed by route inspection via php artisan route:list.

title: Unthrottled Guest Payment Proof Endpoint Allows Phone Verification Brute Force and Spurious Payment Injection
description: The guest payment proof upload endpoint verifies customer identity solely via 4 phone digits without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to brute force the phone verification, upload arbitrary files, and inject spurious pending payments into legitimate transactions.
root_cause: POST /lookup/payment-proof in routes/web.php has no throttle middleware. In TransactionLookupController::storePaymentProof, guest authentication is guarded only by matching phone_last_4 (10,000 combinations, 0000-9999).
intended_behavior: The endpoint must be protected by strict rate limiting (e.g. throttle:5,1) and prevent multiple unauthenticated pending payment proofs from being injected into active transactions.

trace.description: Public POST /lookup/payment-proof route declared without throttle middleware.
Validates 4-digit phone suffix against customer record with no attempt limiting.
Creates Payment record with status 'Menunggu Verifikasi' and stores uploaded proof file.

evidence.description: if ($customerPhone === '' || $last4 !== $validated['phone_last_4']) throws ValidationException without recording rate limit hits.

conditions.description: Unauthenticated guest access from public internet.
Target transaction has an outstanding unpaid balance and a linked customer with phone number.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unauthenticated remote attacker identifies a transaction code (e.g. from receipt, URL, or enumeration) and iterates phone_last_4 from 0000 to 9999.
instructions: Issue repeated POST requests with different 4-digit phone suffixes to /lookup/payment-proof.
When the matching 4 digits are guessed, observe HTTP 302 redirect with payment_proof_success session flash.
Inspect database to confirm a pending payment is created, locking submittable amount for legitimate customer.
execution.observed_result: A pending payment record is created, reducing submittable_amount and injecting unverified file into cashier verification queue without cashier or customer awareness.

remediation.strategy: Apply strict IP and transaction-code rate limiting (e.g. throttle:5,1) on POST /lookup/payment-proof, and record failed phone verification attempts.

likelihood.reason: Publicly accessible endpoint with only 10,000 combinations (0000-9999) and zero rate limiting.

impact.reason: Allows unauthorized manipulation of transaction financial state, denial of legitimate payment submission, and storage flooding.

confidence.reason: Verified by inspecting route definitions and controller logic.

title: Direct Public Access to EC2 Ports 80 and 443 Bypassing Cloudflare Edge Security Controls
description: System documentation states that AWS EC2 security groups open ports 80 and 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 while domain traffic is routed through Cloudflare. If origin IP filtering is absent, attackers can bypass Cloudflare WAF, DDoS protection, and rate limiting by accessing the origin IP directly.
claimed_root_cause: AWS EC2 security group inbound rules permit 0.0.0.0/0 on port 80/443 without restricting ingress to Cloudflare published IP ranges.

trace.description: Security Group Inbound Port 80 and 443 documented as open to 0.0.0.0/0.
Application trusts all proxies, meaning direct requests without Cloudflare headers are processed as originating from untrusted client.

evidence.description: Security Group Inbound: Port 22 (SSH), Port 80 (HTTP), Port 443 (HTTPS) terbuka untuk 0.0.0.0/0.

blockers: AWS EC2 security group live configuration and active Nginx IP allowlist blocks cannot be confirmed solely from source code in the repository.

validation_plan.local: Review Nginx configuration template in docs/sistem.md to confirm whether Cloudflare IP ranges and 'deny all;' directives are configured.
validation_plan.deployment: Log in to AWS EC2 management console; inspect Security Group inbound rules for instance 3.25.167.8 and restrict port 80/443 to Cloudflare IP ranges.

title: Candidate SQL Injection in Transaction Code Lookup via mb_strtoupper
description: Initial hypothesis that passing raw string input into UPPER(transaction_code) = ? could cause SQL injection.

trace.description: Receives raw 'code' query parameter and passes it to whereRaw.
Executes whereRaw with positional parameter binding.

reason: The query uses PDO positional parameter binding ('?'), properly escaping and parameterizing the $code variable. No string concatenation or raw interpolation occurs. The claim is refuted by source analysis.

title: Broken Access Control Allows Operational Staff to Access Executive Financial Reports and Customer PII
description: Operational staff accounts can access confidential administrative financial reports, gross revenue aggregations, and export all customer transaction histories with phone numbers due to overly broad route middleware grouping.
root_cause: In routes/web.php, the /admin/reports routes are enclosed inside Route::middleware('role:admin,staff'), and ReportController methods contain no role authorization checks.
intended_behavior: Administrative reports and financial export routes must be restricted strictly to users with role 'admin'.

trace.description: Route::middleware('role:admin,staff') wraps all staff and admin sub-routes.
Route::get('/reports', [ReportController::class, 'index']) defined inside admin prefix but without role:admin middleware.
Renders financial KPIs, revenue summaries, and full transaction listings without checking user role.

evidence.description: ReportController contains no Gate::authorize, abort(403), or role verification.

conditions.description: Attacker has valid credentials for a staff account (role: 'staff').

execution.attacker_perspective: An authenticated staff user navigates directly to /admin/reports or export endpoints.
instructions: Log in as a user with role 'staff'.
Observe HTTP 200 OK rendering full financial dashboard and export buttons.
execution.observed_result: Staff user successfully views total turnover, revenue KPIs, customer names, phone numbers, and downloads full financial reports.

remediation.strategy: Move ReportController routes into a dedicated Route::middleware('role:admin') group, or add authorization check in ReportController.

likelihood.reason: Any operational staff member can access the URL directly without special tools.

impact.reason: Exposure of sensitive business financial figures and full customer PII database to non-managerial staff.

confidence.reason: Confirmed by route inspection and lack of authorization guards in ReportController.

title: CSV Formula Injection via Unsanitized Customer Names in Operational Transaction Export
description: Exporting transactions to CSV directly interpolates customer names and service summaries into spreadsheet cells without escaping formula trigger characters (=, +, -, @, \t, \r), enabling formula injection or command execution when opened in Excel.
root_cause: ReportController::exportCsv streams raw customer name ($transaction->customer?->name) directly into fputcsv without prefixing an apostrophe or stripping leading formula characters.
intended_behavior: Any cell value starting with '=', '+', '-', '@', tab, or carriage return must be sanitized (e.g. prepended with an apostrophe "'") before CSV output.

trace.description: Customer registers with a custom name containing formula triggers (e.g. =cmd|' /C calc'!A0).
Query retrieves transactions and customer records for export.
fputcsv writes unescaped customer name into CSV stream.

evidence.description: $transaction->customer?->name ?? 'Pelanggan Umum' passed directly to fputcsv without escaping.

conditions.description: Administrator or Owner downloads CSV export and opens it in Microsoft Excel without Protected View.

execution.attacker_perspective: A malicious user registers with name '=1+1' or '=cmd|' /C calc'!A0' and creates an order.
instructions: Register a customer account with name '=1+1'.
Create a laundry transaction for that customer.
As Admin, download CSV export from /admin/reports/export/csv.
Open the CSV file in spreadsheet software.
execution.observed_result: The cell is interpreted as a formula rather than a text string.

remediation.strategy: Sanitize all string values written to CSV by prepending an apostrophe (') if the first character is in ['=', '+', '-', '@', "\t", "\r"].

likelihood.reason: Requires unauthenticated registration with crafted name and an administrator exporting and opening CSV.

impact.reason: Client-side formula execution / arbitrary command execution on administrator workstation via spreadsheet software.

confidence.reason: Confirmed by examining fputcsv payload handling in ReportController.

title: Overly Permissive Proxy Trust Configuration Enables Complete Bypass of IP-Based Rate Limiting
description: Configuring trustProxies(at: '*') causes the application to trust client-supplied X-Forwarded-For headers indiscriminately, allowing attackers to forge arbitrary client IPs and bypass IP-based rate limiting (such as login throttling).
root_cause: bootstrap/app.php configures $middleware->trustProxies(at: '*'). In direct server access or misconfigured reverse proxies, Laravel's getClientIp() reads the leftmost X-Forwarded-For IP supplied by the client.
intended_behavior: trustProxies should specify the exact CIDR blocks of trusted proxies (e.g. Cloudflare IP ranges) or internal reverse proxies, rather than a blanket wildcard.

trace.description: Rate limiter key incorporates $this->ip(), which resolves from untrusted X-Forwarded-For.
RateLimiter check is bypassed for every request with a distinct spoofed IP.

evidence.description: $middleware->trustProxies(at: '*'); sets proxy trust to all IP addresses.

conditions.description: Application is accessible directly or behind a proxy that forwards client-supplied X-Forwarded-For headers.

execution.attacker_perspective: An attacker performs credential stuffing against /login while rotating X-Forwarded-For headers on each request.
instructions: Send 10 failed login attempts with header X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1.
Send an 11th failed login attempt with header X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.2.
Observe that the 11th request is not throttled.
execution.observed_result: Throttle key recalculates with the spoofed IP, resetting the attempt counter and bypassing lockout.

remediation.strategy: Configure trustProxies with explicit Cloudflare IP ranges or trusted internal load balancer IPs instead of wildcard '*'.

likelihood.reason: Any client can supply custom X-Forwarded-For HTTP request headers.

impact.reason: Enables bypass of rate limiting controls, credential stuffing, and IP-based access logs.
